acute-limb-ischaemia
Acute limb ischaemia
urgent
A sudden cold, pale, painful leg or arm. Come to the hospital the same hour, not the next day.

Acute limb ischaemia means the blood supply to an arm or leg has been suddenly cut off, usually by a clot blocking the artery. Without blood flow, the tissue starts to be damaged within hours. This is one of the true emergencies in vascular surgery. The limb, and sometimes life, can depend on how quickly it is treated.
A leg or arm that suddenly turns cold and pale
Sudden, severe pain in the limb
Numbness or weakness that comes on quickly
A pulse that can no longer be felt in the foot or wrist

This is treated as an emergency from the moment you arrive. Dr. Sajjad will assess the limb straight away and act quickly, which may mean an urgent operation to clear the blockage, medicine to break down the clot, or a combination of both, depending on what is found. Every hour matters, so treatment does not wait for a routine appointment slot.
Immediately after treatment: close monitoring in hospital to confirm the blood supply has returned.
First days: the cause of the sudden blockage is investigated, for example the heart or the artery itself.
Weeks: physiotherapy and wound care if any tissue was affected before treatment.
Ongoing: medicine to lower the chance of another clot, and treatment of the underlying cause.
How is this different from ordinary peripheral artery disease?

Peripheral artery disease narrows the artery slowly over years. Acute limb ischaemia is a sudden, complete blockage, usually by a clot, and it is a same hour emergency, not something that can wait for a booked appointment.
What happens if treatment is delayed?

Without blood flow, muscle and nerve tissue can be damaged within hours, and the limb can be lost. This is why a sudden cold, pale, painful leg or arm needs hospital care immediately, not the next day.
What should I do if this happens to me or a family member?
Go to a hospital straight away. Do not wait for a clinic appointment. Tell the hospital staff that a limb has suddenly gone cold, pale and painful, so it is treated as the emergency it is.

diabetic-foot
Diabetic foot and limb salvage
foot
A foot wound that is not healing with diabetes. The blood supply is checked first, then the wound is treated.

Diabetes can damage the nerves in the feet, so you may not feel a small injury. It can also narrow the arteries, so less blood reaches the foot to heal it. A small cut or blister can then turn into a deep wound or infection without you noticing early. This is why a diabetic foot needs to be taken seriously and seen quickly.
A sore, blister or cut on the foot that is not healing
Redness, swelling, warmth or a bad smell from a wound
Numbness, tingling or loss of feeling in the feet
Black or darkening skin on a toe or the foot
Fluid or pus draining from a wound

Care has several parts working together: cleaning and treating the wound, controlling infection, and checking the blood supply. If the arteries are narrowed, they may be opened with a balloon or bypass so blood can reach the wound to heal it. The aim is always to save as much of the foot as possible. Good diabetes control is part of the treatment.
Wounds heal slowly in diabetes, so treatment is often over weeks with regular checks.
Keeping weight off the wound, dressings, and blood sugar control are all essential.
For patients from out of town, some follow-up checks can be done by evening online video call.
The earlier the wound is seen, the better the chance of saving the foot.
Can my foot be saved, or will I lose it?

Many feet can be saved when the wound is treated early and the blood supply is restored. The chance is much better the sooner you come. Dr. Sajjad will be honest with you about what is possible in your case.
Why does a small wound become so dangerous in diabetes?
Diabetes can dull the feeling in the feet and reduce blood flow, so a wound is noticed late and heals slowly. That combination lets a small problem grow into a serious one.
How often will I need to come in?
Diabetic wounds need regular checks, often weekly at first. Some of these can be done online for patients travelling from outside Peshawar, once Dr. Sajjad has seen the foot in person.

dialysis-access
Arteriovenous fistula for dialysis
AV fistula creation and repair
fistula
Creating the fistula in the arm for dialysis, and repairing one that has stopped working.

When the kidneys fail, dialysis does their job of cleaning the blood. For this, the machine needs a strong connection to your blood flow. A small operation joins an artery to a vein in your arm, usually at the wrist or elbow. Over some weeks this vein grows stronger and larger, giving a reliable point for the dialysis needles. This join is called a fistula.
You have been told your kidneys are failing and you will need dialysis
You are on dialysis through a temporary line and need a lasting access
An existing fistula has stopped working, become blocked, or is not developing
Swelling or problems around an old access site

Dr. Sajjad creates the fistula in a small operation, usually with the arm numbed, and you go home the same day. It then takes several weeks to mature (grow strong enough to use). If a fistula stops working, he can often repair it or create a new one, so your dialysis is not interrupted for long.
Day of surgery: a small cut on the arm, mild soreness, home the same day.
First weeks: simple arm exercises as advised help the fistula grow strong.
Six to eight weeks: the fistula usually becomes ready for dialysis needles.
Regular checks make sure it stays healthy and working well.
How long before my fistula can be used for dialysis?
Most fistulas need about six to eight weeks to mature before they are strong enough to use. This is why it is best to have it made in good time, before you urgently need dialysis.
Is creating a fistula a major operation?
No. It is a small operation, usually done with the arm numbed, and you go home the same day.
My old fistula has stopped working. Can it be fixed?
Often yes. Many blocked or failing fistulas can be repaired, or a new access can be created, so your dialysis continues with as little interruption as possible.

dvt
Deep vein thrombosis
Deep vein thrombosis (a blood clot in the leg)
clot
A leg that becomes swollen, warm and painful on one side. Assessed and treated urgently.

Deep vein thrombosis means a blood clot has formed in one of the deep veins, usually in the calf or thigh. The clot blocks the blood trying to return to the heart, so the leg swells and hurts. The main danger is that a piece of the clot can break off and travel to the lungs, which is serious.
Swelling in one leg that comes on over hours or a day or two
Pain or cramp in the calf, often when standing or walking
The skin feeling warm, and looking red or slightly blue
The leg feeling tight and tender to touch

First the clot is confirmed, usually with an ultrasound scan. Treatment is blood-thinning medicine that stops the clot growing and lets the body clear it safely. In selected cases other treatments are used to remove or break down a large clot. You will also be checked to understand why the clot formed.
Early days: blood-thinning medicine is started, and gentle walking is usually encouraged.
Weeks: swelling settles slowly. A support stocking is often advised.
Months: blood thinners are usually continued for a set period, decided for your case.
Follow-up checks make sure the leg is recovering and the medicine dose is right.
Is a blood clot in the leg an emergency?
It should be seen quickly, the same day if possible. A clot can grow or travel to the lungs. If your leg is suddenly swollen and painful, do not wait. Seek care straight away.
How long will I need to take blood thinners?
This depends on why the clot formed. Some people need them for a few months, others for longer. Dr. Sajjad will explain the plan and the reasons for it.
Can I fly or travel with a blood clot?
Long journeys can raise the risk while a clot is active. Ask Dr. Sajjad before making travel plans so he can advise on what is safe for you.

bypass-grafting
Bypass grafting for limb salvage
Bypass graft surgery
bypass
When a blockage is too long to open, blood is routed around it to save the leg.

Some artery blockages are too long or too hard for a balloon and stent to open safely. In these cases, a bypass can be made: a graft, either a vein taken from elsewhere in your body or a synthetic tube, is joined above and below the blockage so blood flows around it, not through it. This restores blood flow to the leg or foot and can prevent amputation.
Leg pain at rest, especially at night, that hangs the foot out of bed for relief
A foot or toe wound that is not healing because the blood supply is poor
Severe cramping pain when walking even a short distance
A cold, pale or discoloured foot with weak or absent pulses

Dr. Sajjad first maps the blockage with scans to see if a bypass is the right option, or whether a balloon and stent can be used instead. If a bypass is needed, it is done as an operation, usually under anaesthesia, joining a graft above and below the blocked section. This is bigger surgery than a balloon procedure, and he will explain honestly what it involves before you agree to it.
First few days: a hospital stay while the leg and wound are monitored closely.
First weeks: swelling in the leg is normal and settles gradually. Gentle walking is encouraged as advised.
One to two months: the graft is checked with follow-up scans to confirm it is working well.
Managing diabetes, blood pressure and stopping smoking all protect the graft afterwards.
Why not just use a balloon and stent instead of a bypass?

A balloon and stent work well for shorter narrowings. When the blockage is too long or too hard, a bypass gives a more reliable route for blood flow. Dr. Sajjad will explain which one fits your scans.
Is bypass surgery safe?

It is a bigger operation than a balloon procedure, and like any surgery it carries risk. It is offered when it gives the best chance of saving the leg, and Dr. Sajjad will discuss the risks and benefits with you and your family before the day of surgery.
How long will I be in hospital?
This varies by case, but a bypass usually means a longer hospital stay than a balloon procedure. You will be given a clear plan for your own recovery before you go home.

peripheral-artery-disease
Peripheral arterial disease
Peripheral artery disease
artery
Pain in the calf when you walk, from narrowed leg arteries. Opened with a balloon and a stent where possible.

Arteries carry fresh blood down to your legs. When they become narrowed or blocked, usually by a slow build-up over years, the muscles cannot get enough blood while you walk. The muscle cramps and forces you to stop. After you rest, the pain eases, then returns when you walk again.
Cramp or ache in the calf or thigh after walking a set distance
The pain easing within a few minutes of stopping
Cold feet, or one foot colder than the other
Slow-healing sores on the foot or toes
In advanced cases, pain in the foot even at rest, especially at night

Treatment starts with medicine, stopping smoking, and a walking programme, which together can improve things a great deal. When the narrowing is severe, the artery can be widened from the inside using a balloon, and a small metal tube called a stent can be placed to hold it open (this is called angioplasty and stenting). Dr. Sajjad will use scans to decide what is right for you.
After a balloon or stent: this is often a day case or a short stay, with a small puncture, not a large cut.
First week: light walking as advised, avoiding heavy strain.
Ongoing: medicine and a walking routine protect the result. Managing diabetes, blood pressure and stopping smoking all matter.
Is angioplasty a big operation?
No. Angioplasty is usually done through a small puncture in the skin, not a large cut. Many patients go home the same day or after a short stay.
Can leg pain when walking be treated without surgery?
Often yes. Medicine, stopping smoking and a steady walking programme improve many patients. Surgery or a balloon is used when the narrowing is severe or the simpler steps are not enough.
What happens if I ignore it?
Untreated, the blood supply can worsen, leading to rest pain, wounds that will not heal, and in the worst cases the risk of losing part of the limb. Seen early, it is much easier to manage.

varicocele
Microsurgical varicocelectomy
Varicocele
microscope
For varicocele, including cases being investigated for difficulty having children. Done under an operating microscope.

A varicocele is a group of swollen veins in the scrotum, a little like varicose veins in the leg. The blood does not drain away properly and pools there. This can raise the temperature around the testicle, which is one reason it can affect the making of healthy sperm and cause fertility problems.
A dull ache or dragging feeling in the scrotum, worse after standing all day
A soft lump that feels like a bag of worms, often on the left side
One side of the scrotum looking or feeling larger
Difficulty with fertility, found during tests for a couple trying for a baby

The swollen veins are tied off so blood drains the correct way. Dr. Sajjad does this under an operating microscope (a special magnifying microscope used during surgery). The magnification lets him find and protect the tiny artery and lymph vessels, which lowers the chance of problems and gives a cleaner result. It is a small operation and most men go home the same day.
First few days: rest, with mild soreness managed by simple pain medicine. Supportive underwear helps.
One week: most men return to office work and light activity.
Two to four weeks: avoid heavy lifting and hard exercise until cleared.
If the operation was for fertility, a sperm test is usually repeated after a few months to check improvement.
Can varicocele surgery improve my chances of having a baby?

For many men, repairing a varicocele improves the quality of the sperm over several months, which can improve the chance of fertility. It cannot be promised for every man. Dr. Sajjad will explain what the surgery can realistically do in your case.
Why use a microscope for the operation?
The microscope magnifies the area so the surgeon can clearly see and protect the tiny artery and other small vessels. This precision lowers the risk of complications and of the problem returning.
Will I be put to sleep for varicocele surgery?
It can be done under general anaesthesia (asleep) or with the area numbed, depending on your case. This is decided and explained with you before the day of surgery.

varicose-veins
Varicose veins and chronic venous disease
Varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency
vein
Aching, swollen, bulging leg veins. Treated with laser inside the vein, or by removing it, depending on the ultrasound.

The veins in your legs carry blood back up to your heart. Small valves inside them stop the blood falling back down. When these valves stop working, blood pools in the lower leg. Over time this shows as swelling, aching and the twisted veins you can see under the skin.
Legs that feel heavy and ache by the end of the day
Swelling around the ankle that is worse in hot weather or after standing
Twisted, rope-like blue or green veins you can see or feel
Itching, or a brown or hard patch of skin near the ankle
In later stages, a wound near the ankle that is slow to heal

For many people the vein is closed from the inside using laser (a thin fibre that seals the faulty vein so blood flows through healthy veins instead). This is usually done while you are awake, with the leg numbed, and you go home the same day. Larger or more advanced veins may need a small operation. Dr. Sajjad will examine your legs, often with an ultrasound scan, and tell you which option fits you.
Day of treatment: you can walk straight away, and walking is encouraged.
First week: some bruising and tightness is normal. Simple pain medicine is enough. You wear a support stocking as advised.
One to two weeks: most people are back to normal daily life and office work.
Heavy physical work may need a little longer. You will be given a clear plan.
Is laser treatment for varicose veins painful?

There is very little pain. The leg is numbed first, so during the treatment you feel pressure more than pain. Afterwards there may be mild soreness and bruising for a few days, managed with simple pain medicine.
Will my varicose veins come back after treatment?
The treated vein is sealed for good. New veins can sometimes appear over the years, but a good result usually lasts a long time. Wearing support stockings when advised and staying active both help.
How much does varicose vein treatment cost in Peshawar?
The cost depends on how many veins are involved and whether laser or surgery is used. Fees are explained openly before treatment, with no hidden charges. Please feel free to ask.

Varicose veins are one of the most common reasons patients come to see Dr. Sajjad. Many have lived with heavy, aching legs for years, thinking nothing can be done. In most cases a great deal can be done, often as a simple day treatment.

varicose-veins-farmer
Back on his feet after years of heavy, aching legs
Charsadda
A farmer in his fifties who had put up with heavy, aching legs and swollen ankles for years. By evening he could barely stand at work, and he had large twisted veins on his lower leg.
An ultrasound scan showed the valves in one of the main leg veins were not working, so blood was pooling in the lower leg. The skin near his ankle had started to darken.
The faulty vein was closed from the inside using laser, as a day case with the leg numbed. He walked out the same day.
The heavy, aching feeling settled over the following weeks and the ankle swelling improved. The skin colour stopped getting worse.
Back to light work within a few days, and full farm work within about two weeks.
This story is shared with the patient's permission. No identifying details are included. Results vary from person to person.

pain-hurt
Will the treatment hurt?

Most vein treatments cause little pain. You are given medicine so the area is numb, and you can go home the same day. For bigger operations you are given anaesthesia so you feel nothing during the surgery. Some soreness afterwards is normal and is managed with simple pain medicine. Dr. Sajjad will tell you honestly what to expect for your own case before anything is done.

pain-asleep
Will I be put to sleep?

It depends on the treatment. Many vein procedures are done while you are awake, with only the leg numbed. Larger operations may need general anaesthesia, which means you are asleep and feel nothing. This is always explained and agreed with you first.
recovery-work
How long until I can walk and go back to work?

For most vein treatments you can walk the same day, and light walking is encouraged. Many people return to office work within a few days. Heavier physical work may need one to two weeks. Recovery is different for every person and every procedure, so you will be given a clear plan for your own situation.
Recovery
recovery-overnight
Do I need to stay overnight in hospital?

Many vascular treatments are day cases, which means you come in and go home the same day. Some larger operations need a short hospital stay. You will know which one applies to you before the day of treatment, so you can arrange things at home.
recovery-return
Will the problem come back?

For most conditions, proper treatment gives a lasting result, but no honest doctor can promise a problem will never return. A lot depends on the condition and on care afterwards, such as managing diabetes or wearing support stockings when advised. Dr. Sajjad will explain the real chances for your case, without over-promising.
cost
How much does it cost?

Fees are discussed openly and clearly before any treatment, with no hidden charges. The cost depends on the condition and the treatment needed. If you are worried about cost, please raise it. It is a normal and fair question, and it will be answered plainly.

profile
Known as the Rescue Surgeon, a specialist for blood vessel problems in Peshawar, with over ten years in surgery at the largest hospital in the province.
Lady Reading Hospital MTI, Peshawar
Lady Reading Hospital is a teaching hospital with more than 1,800 beds. It was started in 1924 and is one of the main hospitals that the whole province is sent to for serious cases.

Dr. Sajjad Yousafzai is a vascular surgeon, known to many patients as the Rescue Surgeon. That means he treats problems with the blood vessels: the veins and arteries that carry blood around your body. He also does general and keyhole (laparoscopic) surgery.

Dr. Sajjad Yousafzai works across endovascular surgery (treating blood vessels from inside, without large cuts) and microvascular surgery (operating under magnification on very small vessels). He is a superspecialist in varicocele microscopic surgery, a fine, precise operation for male infertility caused by swollen veins in the scrotum.

He has spent more than ten years in surgery. About six of those years were in general surgery, and the last four have been given fully to vascular work. He treats these problems every week, so they are not unusual to him.

He works as a Consultant Vascular and General Surgeon at Lady Reading Hospital in Peshawar, the biggest hospital in the province. He also sees patients privately at Pak Medical Center in Khyber Bazar.

Patients say the same thing again and again: he takes his time, he explains what is wrong in words you can follow, and he does not rush you out of the room. Some of his patients are sent to him by other doctors who trust him with their own cases.
I want you to leave my room understanding your own body. If you know what is wrong and why, the treatment makes sense and you are not frightened.
